what_it_does: Modern processors have many independent computing cores that all share the same pool of memory bandwidth; each core can try to speculatively fetch data before it is needed (called prefetching), but if every core greedily prefetches as aggressively as possible, they collectively jam the shared memory bus and everyone slows down. MAMA treats each core's prefetcher as an independent learning agent — like a player in a game — that adjusts how aggressively it prefetches based on rewards tied to performance. To prevent the agents from fighting each other, a lightweight central supervisor with a view of the whole system's memory bandwidth steers them toward a cooperative strategy. Local agents first narrow down their choices to a small set of reasonable options, and the supervisor then picks among those combined choices, avoiding the explosion of possibilities that would occur if it had to consider every option for every core simultaneously.
